title: Design a distributed caching system like Redis or Memcached.
description: High-availability distributed cache with consistent hashing, replication, and eviction policies.

data.text: **Question:** Design a distributed caching system like Redis or Memcached.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: High availability with automatic failover
Data consistency across cache replicas
Configurable eviction policies (LRU, LFU, TTL)
Support for large values and bulk operations
Cluster mode for horizontal scaling
Pub/sub for cache invalidation events

data.title: Scale Assumptions
items: 1 million QPS across all cache nodes
100 terabytes of cached data
Average object size: 1 kilobyte
99.99% availability target
P99 latency under 1 millisecond
10% cache miss rate acceptable

data.text: The system uses consistent hashing to distribute keys across cache nodes. Each node maintains a primary replica and one or more secondary replicas for high availability. A gossip protocol monitors node health and triggers failover. An eviction engine runs periodically to enforce memory limits using the configured policy.

data.title: Consistent Hashing
data.text: Use virtual nodes in consistent hashing to evenly distribute keys when nodes are added or removed. This minimizes data movement during cluster changes.

data.title: Memory Management Strategies
items: LRU (Least Recently Used): Evicts items not accessed recently
LFU (Least Frequently Used): Evicts items with low access counts
TTL-based: Expires items after a time-to-live duration
Random: Evicts random items for simplicity under high load
Size-based: Prioritizes evicting large objects first

data.text: Choose between strong consistency, eventual consistency, and session consistency based on use case. Strong consistency ensures all replicas return the same value but increases latency. Eventual consistency allows replicas to diverge temporarily but provides lower latency and higher availability.

data.title: Cache Consistency
data.text: Use write-through or write-behind strategies to keep cache consistent with the source of truth. Write-through ensures consistency but adds write latency. Write-behind improves write throughput but risks data loss.

cards.title: Strong Consistency
cards.description: All reads return the most recent write. Requires quorum writes.

cards.title: Eventual Consistency
cards.description: Replicas converge over time. Reads may return stale data.

cards.title: Session Consistency
cards.description: Within a session, reads see their own writes. Balances consistency and performance.

data.title: Horizontal Scaling Strategies
items: Use consistent hashing with virtual nodes for even distribution
Add read replicas to handle read-heavy workloads
Partition data by key prefix for isolation
Use proxy layer to abstract cluster topology from clients
Monitor hit ratio and eviction rates to tune memory allocation

items.question: How do you handle cache stampedes?
items.answer: Use cache locks, request coalescing, or probabilistic early expiration. Distribute cache expiry times to avoid thundering herds.

items.question: How do you handle node failures?
items.answer: Use automatic failover to replicas. Consistent hashing redistributes only the failed node's keys, minimizing impact on other nodes.

items.question: How do you handle cache warming?
items.answer: Preload hot keys after node restarts or deployments. Use background jobs to rebuild caches gradually to avoid overwhelming the database.

items.question: What is the optimal cache size?
items.answer: Size the cache to hold the working set with a 10-20% buffer. Monitor hit ratio and eviction rate. A hit ratio below 80% suggests the cache is too small.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes minimizes data movement
Replication provides high availability but requires consistency trade-offs
Eviction policies should match access patterns (LRU for recency, LFU for frequency)
Cache stampedes require proactive mitigation strategies
Monitor hit ratio and eviction rate to size caches correctly
data.takeaway: Distributed caches require careful trade-offs between consistency, availability, and memory efficiency through consistent hashing and replication.
